findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` runs `where(email: value)` on the raw value. At validation time the user's email has not been downcased or normalized, so `Bad@Spammers.org` will not match a stored `bad@spammers.org`. A blocked address can register just by changing the letter case.

findings.title: Match counter updated with racy read-modify-write during validation
findings.body: `should_block?` loads the record, increments `match_count` in Ruby and saves it. Concurrent requests for the same address lose increments. It also writes to the database on every `valid?` call, so the count is inflated: `UsersController#create` validates twice (once in `user.valid?`, once in `save`). An atomic `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1')` would avoid the race.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is shared across controller instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared in the prototype passed to `extend`, so every instance shares the same array. Rejected emails therefore persist across modal reopenings and across controller instances instead of being per-instance state. It should be initialized in `init`.

findings.title: Any email error permanently rejects the address client-side
findings.body: The client records the email as rejected on any email error, including a transient one such as a uniqueness conflict. That address then can never be resubmitted from the form. The reason shown is also the generic "invalid" message, not the server's actual error.

findings.title: Whitelist/blacklist behavior moved without tests
findings.body: The domain whitelist/blacklist logic was moved out of `User` into `EmailValidator`, but the new spec only covers the blocked-email path. The moved logic has no coverage. There is also no test that a whitelist or blacklist failure skips the blocked-email check.
